application_type_full: Tree works: Trees in conservation areas/subject to TPOs
description:
Quercus ilex (Holm Oak) T1 on the sketch plan  (51KG-01 Sketch plan.JPG). Front garden of number 51 Kew Green.
Proposed reduction of crown (51KG-07 Requested size.JPG) to the height of the parapet of the property, a reduction of approximately 3m and reduced in width/spread by 2m on all sides away from building, and up to 1m on the building side where it has grown less due to the building shadow and north facing aspect.
Proposed removal of the lower limb (51KG-03 Front view, lower limb.jpeg) 

Reasons for work: 
The Quercus ilex is now dwarfing the property and limiting light, (51KG-02 Elevation view.jpeg) The Quercus ilex is overhanging the pavement and road, branches are frequently snapped off by coaches on Kew Green (51KG-04 Elevation view with Coach.jpeg). 
Quercus ilex is a large landscape tree,  a suitable size for the neighbouring RBG Kew and Kew Green itself. It is out of context as a domestic tree in this setting.(51KG-06 wider view.jpeg) It is likely that this tree was never intended to be grown in this position. (51kg-05 Historic view from KG.JPG).  The large landscape trees in the landscape are all either on Kew Green itself, or borrowed landscape from RBG Kew.  None of the domestic settings have trees of this size in their front gardens, being limited to cherries and olives of between 2.5m-4m tall. 
The householders would like to keep the existing tree, as per the TPO, but at a size that is more suitable for its setting, not interfering with the house, pavement, or public highway.
decision_conditions: The application has been refused due to insufficient justification for the proposed works, in particular the removal of the lower limb, for which no supporting arboricultural justification has been provided. The proposed crown reduction is excessive in scale and would result in large pruning wounds, likely to have a detrimental impact on the health and structural integrity of the tree and increase its susceptibility to pests and disease. The extent of the proposed works would also significantly reduce the tree’s contribution to local public amenity.
